interviewQuestions.question: How do you approach the Buy/Sell Stock problem when unlimited transactions are allowed?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd model each day as being in one of two states — holding a share, or not — and notice that with unlimited, cost-free transactions, the optimal strategy collapses to something simple: capture every single profitable day-over-day move.

Concretely: `profit = sum of (prices[i] - prices[i-1]) for every i where prices[i] > prices[i-1])`. The reasoning is that any multi-day upward run can be decomposed into its daily increments without losing anything — buying at the start of a run and selling at the end nets exactly the sum of each day's gain along the way, and because there's no cap on transactions and no fee, there's zero cost to slicing one big win into many small buy/sell pairs that each capture one day's delta.

I'd implement it as a single O(n) pass with O(1) space, tracking nothing but a running profit total. I'd also flag proactively that this greedy shortcut is specific to the *unlimited, unconstrained* case — the moment a cooldown, fee, or transaction cap gets added, this exact logic no longer holds and I'd need to go back to explicit hold/not-hold state tracking.

**Testing:** whether you can explain *why* the greedy approach is valid here specifically, rather than just reciting that it works.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Now add a mandatory one-day cooldown after every sell before you can buy again. How does your approach change?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The two-state model — holding or not holding — is no longer enough, because 'not holding' now needs to distinguish two genuinely different situations: just sold and still in cooldown, versus free to buy right now. So I add a third explicit state.

Three states per day: `hold` (holding a share), `sold` (just sold today, in cooldown), and `rest` (not holding, cooldown has passed, free to buy). The transitions: `hold[i] = max(hold[i-1], rest[i-1] - price[i])` — you can only enter `hold` by buying from `rest`, never directly from `sold`, since that's the whole point of the cooldown. `sold[i] = hold[i-1] + price[i]` — selling today. `rest[i] = max(rest[i-1], sold[i-1])` — you're resting if you were already resting, or if yesterday was your cooldown day.

The answer at the end is `max(sold[n-1], rest[n-1])` — you'd never want to end holding a share you can't cash in.

The general principle I'd name explicitly: a new constraint on a *transition* (you can't buy the day right after selling) usually means the state space itself needs a new state to represent the constrained condition, not just a patched-up recurrence on the old two states.

**Testing:** whether you can extend a state machine cleanly by adding a state for a genuinely new condition, rather than trying to hack the constraint into existing transitions.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Variants

interviewQuestions.question: How would you handle at most k transactions, and what happens as k grows very large?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd extend the state to include how many transactions have been used: `hold[i][t]` and `sold[i][t]`, meaning the best profit ending day `i` in that holding status having used exactly `t` transactions (or up to `t`, depending on how I define it). A sell completes a transaction, so it draws from the hold state at `t-1`: `sold[i][t] = max(sold[i-1][t], hold[i-1][t-1] + price[i])`; a buy just carries the count forward: `hold[i][t] = max(hold[i-1][t], sold[i-1][t] - price[i])`.

This gives O(n*k) states, each O(1) to compute, and it collapses to O(k) space since each day only reads the previous day's row.

The interesting edge case is what happens as `k` grows: once `k >= n/2`, you can never actually run out of transactions — there aren't enough days to use more than `n/2` buy/sell pairs anyway — so the cap becomes meaningless and the problem degenerates back to the unlimited-transactions case. A good implementation checks for this and falls back to the O(n) greedy-sum solution when `k` is large, both because it's faster and because the O(n*k) formulation can become needlessly expensive or even numerically awkward for very large k values that don't add any real constraint.

**Testing:** whether you extend the state machine correctly for a bounded resource, and whether you catch the large-k degenerate case rather than blindly running an O(n*k) solution regardless of k's size.
